blogs.title: The Objective Observer in Fair Use: Why Subjective Intent Doesn't Save Santos
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Second Circuit's rigorous application of the 'transformative use' test in *Santos v. Kimmel*, specifically focusing on the court's rejection of the argument that a defendant's deceptive conduct (Kimmel using pseudonyms) negates fair use. The piece will dissect the panel's reliance on *Andy Warhol Foundation v. Goldsmith* to establish that the 'reasonable observer' standard, rather than the subjective intent of either party, dictates whether a work is transformative. It will explore how this ruling clarifies the role of 'bad faith' in modern fair use jurisprudence, distinguishing between deceptive procurement and the ultimate expressive purpose of the secondary work.

blogs.title: Pleading Fair Use at 12(b)(6): When Deception Becomes Commentary
blogs.description: While many fair use battles end in summary judgment, *Santos v. Kimmel* reaffirms that fair use can sometimes be dispositive at the motion-to-dismiss stage. This article examines the procedural significance of dismissing Santos's copyright claim before discovery, arguing that the court found the 'transformative' nature of Kimmel's satire so evident on the face of the complaint that no factual development was needed. The post will contrast this outcome with recent debates over when courts should defer to juries versus deciding fair use as a matter of law, highlighting how public figures seeking to monetize their likeness via platforms like Cameo face steep hurdles when their content is repurposed for political or social critique.

blogs.title: The Limits of Third-Party Beneficiary Status: Why Contract Claims Failed Against Cameo Users
blogs.description: Beyond copyright, this post scrutinizes the Second Circuit's dismissal of Santos's state law contract claims, offering a practical lesson for litigants attempting to enforce Terms of Service (ToS) as third-party beneficiaries. The analysis will break down why neither Illinois nor New York law supported Santos's position: under Illinois law, there was no express intent to benefit non-contracting video providers, and under NY law, there was no evidence of a 'meeting of minds' regarding adherence to those specific terms. This section serves as a cautionary tale for digital platform creators who assume platform rules automatically create binding contractual obligations between independent service providers and users.
